work.text: Aside from landscapes, Ma's surviving oeuvre includes many different types of works. These include a number of delicate flower paintings (National Palace Museum, Taipei), a series of paintings of water and mountains (Palace Museum, Beijing) …
His touch is rather clear, hard and firm, not getting [effects] by accident, but by complete mastery over design.

moment.text: Even the very skilful painters did no more than make the tops of the waves rising and falling; men could almost touch them with their hands and feel the heights and the hollows. They are said to be wonderful; yet, they are little better than prints from wooden blocks.
moment.lead: A century before Ma Yuan, the poet-painter Su Shi on how painters drew water (trans. Osvald Sirén):

source.author: Su Shi (Su Tung-p‘o), trans. Osvald Sirén
source.title: A History of Early Chinese Painting, vol. II

matters.text: Water is a thing alive; its appearance may be quiet and deep, soft and smooth; it may be like the big ocean, or it may be winding and curving. It may be unctuous and glossy, or sprinkling and bubbling, dashing like arrows. … Such are the living aspects of water.
